##  {#title-slide background="../images/priors.png" background-size="50%" background-position="50% 20%"}

::: title-box
<h2>Bayesian statistics for ecology</h2>
<h3>Day 3: Mother trees and information sharing</h3>
<p>AFEC-X 2026 · 23 October</p>
<h3>Masatoshi Katabuchi @ XTBG, CAS</h3>

## Survival, density and group differences

- Day 1: uncertainty about a survival probability.
- Day 2: survival probability changes with conspecific density.
- Today: mother trees and species can differ while sharing information.

::: notes
We first leave out the density predictor and use a separate data set to make the
idea of information sharing easier to see. We return to species CNDD later.
:::

## Today's objectives

- Explain complete pooling, separate estimation and partial pooling using a figure.
- Explain why some estimates respond more to shared information.
- Describe where information sharing could help in your own research.

## Eight mother trees

::: columns
::: {.column width="42%"}
```{r tree-data}
trees |> select(tree,n,suv) |> knitr::kable(format="html") |>
  kableExtra::kable_styling(font_size=27)
```
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}

We followed seedlings under eight mother trees of one species.

What survival probability would you report for each mother tree?

Would a hypothetical 0/2 or 2/2 justify complete certainty about survival?
:::
:::

::: notes
These are simulated mother-tree data, different from Day 2's quadrats. The 0/2
and 2/2 counts are hypothetical questions, not rows of this table.
Focus on n and survivors. Hide p_true until after interpretation.
:::

## Separate observed proportions

```{r observed-trees, fig.width=11, fig.height=4.6}
ggplot(trees,aes(tree,suv/n,size=n))+geom_point(shape=21,fill="white",stroke=1.2)+
  ylim(0,1)+labs(x="Mother tree",y="Observed proportion surviving",size="Seedlings")
```

Which differences could reflect sampling variation?

::: notes
10-25 minutes. These are observed proportions, equal to separate binomial MLEs.
The posterior comparison later uses means with explicitly stated priors.
:::

## Complete pooling

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](../images/pool.png){height=340}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

$$s_j\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n_j,p)$$

Every mother tree shares the same $p$.

What ecological difference does this assumption leave out?
:::
:::

::: notes
j indexes mother trees. Our comparison uses p ~ Beta(1,1), the flat Day 1 prior.
An uncertainty interval for a common p does not represent between-tree variation.
:::

## Separate estimation

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](../images/separate.png){height=340}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

$$s_j\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n_j,p_j)$$

Each mother tree has its own independent $p_j$.

How much can a tree with few seedlings tell us on its own?
:::
:::

::: notes
Our comparison uses independent Beta(1,1) priors. What we learn about tree A
does not update the probability for tree B. Small data can give wide intervals.
:::

## Information sharing through a prior

::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](../images/multilevel.png){height=340}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

$$s_j\sim\operatorname{Binomial}(n_j,p_j)$$
$$\operatorname{logit}(p_j)\sim\mathcal{N}(\mu,\sigma)$$

Each mother tree can differ. Their shared distribution describes the commonality.
:::
:::

::: notes
25-40 minutes. A hierarchical prior connects group parameters.
The model estimates mu and sigma from all eight trees, with hyperpriors.
The Normal second argument is SD, on the logit scale.
:::

## The group variation matters

```{r group-variation, fig.width=13, fig.height=4.7}
plot_group_spread()
```

Greater inferred variation generally allows less sharing among mother trees.

::: notes
This illustration fixes mu=0 and changes sigma. It uses fixed Normal quantiles
and shows probabilities, not a density transformed without a Jacobian.
These hypothetical values are not the fitted rates of our trees.
:::

## The completed model and its assumptions

Selected lines from `stan/logistic.stan`:

```stan
mu ~ normal(0, 5);
sigma ~ std_normal();  // sigma is constrained to be positive
z_tilde ~ std_normal();
z = mu + sigma * z_tilde;
// For every mother tree i:
suv[i] ~ binomial_logit(N[i], z[ii[i]]);
```

Data: seedlings and survivors. Unknowns: tree effects, group centre and group SD.

::: notes
These lines come from stan/logistic.stan, shown together for reading. z is a
transformed parameter and sigma has lower bound zero. Read the complete file
in the handout. No independent coding or non-centred parameterisation lesson.
Priors: mu Normal(0,5), sigma half-Normal(0,1). z_tilde is standard Normal.
:::

## Three ways of estimating survival

```{r fitted-trees, fig.width=12, fig.height=4.7}
plot_mother_comparison(comparison)
```

Points: posterior means. Bars: 90% intervals.

::: notes
Complete and separate models use Beta(1,1) probability priors, whereas partial
pooling uses the Normal logit group prior with estimated centre and SD.
State this difference. It is an illustrative model comparison, not an isolation
of pooling under identical marginal priors. All code and priors are in the handout.
:::

## Why estimates move by different amounts

```{r movement, fig.width=12, fig.height=4.5}
plot_mother_movement(comparison)
```

Consider information within a tree, its position in the group distribution, and inferred group variation.

::: notes
Debrief. Avoid saying every estimate moves to the pooled proportion or has a
narrower interval. Shrinkage depends on assumptions and data. It cannot guarantee
smaller estimation error for each group.
:::

## Species differences in CNDD

```{r species-cndd, fig.width=11, fig.height=4.5}
plot_cndd_species()
```

Day 2's common curve becomes a set of species curves.
How could rare species borrow information?

::: footer
Conceptual simulation inspired by [Comita et al. 2010](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1190772)
and [Song & Katabuchi et al. 2024](https://doi.org/10.1002/ecy.4382).
:::

::: notes
55-65 minutes. This is the seeded conceptual example from main.qmd, not fitted
species effects for Day 2's data or a numerical reproduction of either paper.
Mother trees and species are different groups. Individual predictors may also differ.
:::

## Individual and species questions

**Individual level:** how does survival vary with conspecific density?

$$\operatorname{logit}(p_{ij})=\alpha_j+\beta_j x_{ij}$$

**Species level:** do density coefficients vary with species abundance?

$$\beta_j\sim\mathcal{N}(\gamma_0+\gamma_1 a_j,\tau)$$

::: notes
i indexes seedlings and j species here. The response is Bernoulli per seedling,
or binomial when counts share the same predictors. a_j is scaled species abundance.
The group SD tau and all coefficients require priors in a full analysis.
These equations explain structure. They are not another implementation exercise.
:::

## A species-level relationship

```{r species-abundance, fig.width=11, fig.height=4.5}
plot_cndd_abundance()
```

What would this relationship imply about species differences?

::: notes
Simulated coefficients, with the generating line shown. Higher coefficients
here mean less negative slopes. A logit coefficient is not a fixed probability
difference, which also depends on baseline survival and the densities compared.
The model asks about an association. It alone does not establish the cause of rarity.
:::

## Allometry and wood density

::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
```{r allometry-curves, fig.width=8, fig.height=4.6}
allo <- make_allometry_data()
ggplot(allo,aes(dbh,h,colour=sp))+geom_point(alpha=.6)+
  labs(x="DBH (cm)",y="Height (m)")+guides(colour="none")
```
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}

**Individual level:** DBH predicts height.

**Species level:** wood density may predict the allometric exponent.

$$h=a\,\mathrm{DBH}^{b}$$
:::
:::

::: notes
65-70 minutes: optional second research connection, 5 minutes total for two slides.
The data are simulated. Explain the power-law shape visually, without a new
transformation or coefficient exercise. Inspiration follows main.qmd's research
example; its unpublished citation status has not been independently established.
:::

## The same structure with a different response

```{r wood-density, fig.width=11, fig.height=4.5}
plot_wood_density()
```

The response changes to log height. Species still share information through a group model.

::: notes
The figure uses day3_vslope, fitted to the existing simulated allometry data.
Points summarise species exponents and the line summarises their expected value
at each wood density, with 90% intervals. It is not evidence from a real forest.
Skip these two slides if delayed. Detailed transformation and implementation are optional.
:::

## Computation and observations both matter

```{r mother-check, fig.width=12, fig.height=4.5}
plot_mother_check(fit)
```

Does the model reproduce survival counts by mother tree?

::: notes
70-80 minutes. First inspect stored R-hat, bulk/tail ESS, traces, divergences,
treedepth and E-BFMI in the result sheet. Then discuss this predictive check.
Draws use observed n_j and posterior p_j. A good fit is one part of assessment.
:::

## Ecological reasons to share information

Which trees or species belong in a common group distribution?

- Similarity needs an ecological argument.
- Measured group differences can help explain systematic variation.
- Checking by group can reveal patterns hidden in overall summaries.

::: notes
A hierarchical model is not automatically appropriate because a grouping label
exists. Discuss shared habitat, census interval and missing predictors.
:::

## Your own research

Name a grouping and a quantity that may vary among its groups.

What would justify sharing information, and what predicted pattern would you check?

::: notes
80-85 minutes: pairs explain one application in words. Ask two pairs to share.
This is reflection rather than another code exercise. Keep 85-90 for questions.
:::

## Three days of Bayesian thinking

- A posterior expresses uncertainty conditional on data and assumptions.
- Predictions put that uncertainty on the scale of an ecological question.
- Hierarchical priors share information while allowing groups to differ.
- Computation, model-generated data and ecological context all inform interpretation.

# Optional reference {visibility="uncounted"}

## A new mother tree {visibility="uncounted"}

```{r echo=TRUE, eval=FALSE}
set.seed(20261026)
draws <- fit$draws
p_new <- plogis(rnorm(nrow(draws),draws$mu,draws$sigma))
quantile(p_new,c(.05,.5,.95))
```

This predicts a new tree's probability, including group variation. A future
survivor count would also require a seedling count and binomial sampling.
